title: Red-Team Your Own Agent — prompt-injection CI from the jailbreak corpus
thesis: The catalog holds both halves of a loop nobody has closed. On one side sit offense corpora and autonomous attackers — L1B3RT4S still landing on GPT-5, an agent that goes from one sentence to a verified exploit, scanners hunting exposed AI servers. On the other sit the pipes that pour untrusted text into your agent — Agent Reach reading Reddit and X, 90k-skill hubs, one-command skill installers. Point the attacker inward and you get prompt-injection CI — every skill install and harness change gets replayed against a jailbreak-and-hijack suite before it touches your keys.
why_it_matters: Solo builders now run agents with real API keys, inboxes and broker access, and Noma's research shows most automations hand data to anyone who simply asks. Whoever ships a cheap, repeatable injection test owns the trust layer for every one-person agent shop — and sleeps through their own cron jobs.
novelty: Standard practice is a static .env and hope. The catalog shows security posts (exposed OpenAI keys, secrets pasted into chat history) and agent-skill posts from entirely different creators who never reference each other — no one treats the skill supply chain as the attack surface or tests it continuously.

action_sketch: Build a 50-case suite this week — 20 L1B3RT4S-style jailbreaks, 20 Noma-style 'just ask for the data' hijacks planted in fake Reddit/X posts fetched via Agent Reach, 10 sponsored-option nudges — and run it against your harness with a canary secret in the environment

Wire it as a pre-install hook: any new skill from find-skills or a skills hub gets diffed, then the suite reruns with that skill loaded; fail the install if the canary leaks or a tool call goes outside the allowlist
Add the sandboxing layer from the portfolio-projects post — per-skill capability manifests (network, filesystem, secrets) — and measure how many suite cases each manifest blocks
Falsifier: if a plain allowlist on outbound tool calls blocks ≥95% of the suite with no skill-level testing, the CI layer is overkill and a static policy file is the whole answer
prerequisites: An agent harness with hooks (Claude Code or similar)
A throwaway canary secret and a disposable test account
Test only harnesses, accounts and keys you own

title: Skills That Earn Their Lines — benchmark-gated self-editing plus subtraction
thesis: Successor to the harness and second-brain dives. Those stop at 'append a lesson after every mistake'. The catalog now holds the missing machinery — Microsoft SkillOpt rewrites skills only when a benchmark improves, bilevel autoresearch adds a coach loop over the worker, Prime Agent rewrites its own harness to 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3 — and, crucially, evidence that subtraction matters as much as addition: Boris Cherny's simple mode and the setup-purge post show stale rules make newer models dumber. Combine them into a ratchet that both adds and deletes rules, keeping only edits that beat a held-out eval.
why_it_matters: Every power user's CLAUDE.md grows monotonically until it is a tax on every call. A two-way, eval-gated ratchet turns rule accretion into measured improvement, and the winning traces become fine-tuning data you can push into a small local model with Soup.
novelty: Standard practice is lessons.md that only grows. The catalog's self-improvement posts (SkillOpt, autoresearch, issue-logging skills) all optimize by adding; the ablation posts (simple mode, purge) never connect to an automated loop. Nobody runs ablation as a gated step.

action_sketch: Export your last 3 months of Claude history, have a small model tag 40 representative tasks with pass/fail criteria — that is your held-out eval
Run an ablation sweep: drop each CLAUDE.md rule and skill one at a time, rerun the eval, delete anything whose removal does not hurt the score
Add the SkillOpt loop on a nightly cron — skills log issues, an optimizer proposes edits, only score-improving edits merge; export passing traces for a Soup fine-tune later
Falsifier: if eval scores vary more between two identical runs than between best and worst rule sets, your eval is too noisy and the whole ratchet is optimizing noise
prerequisites: A CLAUDE.md and skills folder with some history
A cheap model for grading (Haiku-class or local)

title: Earned Autonomy — a three-tier router that demotes work to your own GPU
thesis: Three trends in the catalog point at one design. Orchestrator-worker splits (Fable plans, Opus or GPT-5.6 executes) cut frontier spend. A 27B Qwen now fits a single 24GB card and posts agentic benchmarks that were frontier-only a year ago, while open-token share flipped to 80/20 in twelve weeks. And vendors can change the deal overnight — Anthropic killed subscription tokens in third-party tools. The agentic OS blueprint's 'earned autonomy' is the missing link: let each task class graduate down the stack — frontier, mid-tier, local — as its review pass rate proves it can.
why_it_matters: You stop paying frontier prices for work a local model already passes, and you hedge against any single vendor's terms. The router doubles as a measurement instrument — it tells you, per task class, exactly where the open models have caught up.
novelty: Existing routing posts hard-code the split (big model plans, smaller one builds). None let the split move based on observed pass rates, and none include a local tier as a first-class worker. The local-model posts and routing posts come from different creators and never cite each other.

Stand up Qwen 27B via llama.cpp or Ollama behind the same subagent interface; route one low-stakes class to it in shadow mode and grade it with the same frontier reviewer
Add the promotion rule: 20 consecutive passes moves a class one tier down, any fail moves it back up; track dollars saved per class
Falsifier: if after a month no task class sustains a 90%+ pass rate on the local tier, the local floor is not there yet for your work — stay two-tier
prerequisites: A 24GB GPU or a unified-memory machine

title: Every App Is Headless Now — agents that build their own control surface
thesis: Chamath's claim that software IP stops being a moat once agents call services via MCP assumes the service ships an MCP. The catalog quietly shows you no longer need its permission. 'Build yourself a CLI for this program' covers apps with no API, Reverse Engineer Anything and the Ghidra-backed REA MCP explain closed binaries, and Claude Code already strips a smart TV over WiFi. Put these together and any legacy or closed tool becomes agent-drivable — and Bending Spoons' acquire-and-rebuild playbook shows what that is worth when the software is stagnant.
why_it_matters: The long tail of MCP-less software — dental scheduling suites, MLS portals, ancient ERPs — is where small businesses lose hours. Whoever can wrap one in a reliable agent-built CLI sells the finished work rather than the software, which is exactly the AI-native-service model YC is asking for.
novelty: Standard practice waits for vendors to publish MCP servers. The reverse-engineering posts sit in security and gaming contexts, the 'build a CLI' tip in agent tips, and the headless-software thesis in business news — no entry connects RE tooling to wrapping SMB software as a service.

For the stubborn actions, run Reverse Engineer Anything (or REA MCP for native binaries) to find the underlying file formats or local endpoints, and replace UI clicks with direct calls
Wrap the CLI as an MCP server, run a week of real tasks through it, and price the result as a monthly 'we run it for you' service

title: Mission Control for 80 Agents — Conway's law meets game UI
thesis: Once you run more than a handful of agents, the bottleneck is your attention, not tokens. Creative technologists are already prototyping the answer without naming it — Bot Crossing puts 80 agents on a tiny planet where they raise hands for help, AgentCraft runs them as Minecraft workers in isolated worktrees, a TouchDesigner sketch commands agents by gesture, a Quest 3 canvas directs them spatially. Casey Muratori's point that Conway's law now applies to agents says the interface and the agent org chart are the same design problem. Feed a Booking.com-style trace bus into a game-engine front end and you get a control room where structure is visible.
why_it_matters: Solo operators running Founder-OS-style setups spend their day polling terminals. A spatial view that surfaces only blocked agents, and whose layout mirrors how work is partitioned, lets one person supervise ten times more agents without reading every log.
novelty: Agent dashboards in the catalog are text panels and notch widgets; the game and gesture prototypes are mostly non-functional art. Nobody has wired real tracing into the playful front ends, and nobody has used Conway's law to decide which agents should sit next to each other.

Point Bot Crossing (or a 200-line Three.js scene) at that queue so blocked agents visibly raise hands; cluster agents by the repo/module they own to make the Conway structure visible
Run a week with dashboard versus without and log minutes-to-unblock per blocked agent
Falsifier: if minutes-to-unblock does not drop by at least a third versus a plain notification, the game layer is decoration and a notch widget wins
prerequisites: Willingness to treat this as an art-tech experiment first

title: Dox Yourself First — a scheduled agent that runs the OSINT kit on you
thesis: The catalog saved a full attacker toolkit — Sherlock and Alien's Eye for usernames, email-to-account mappers, deleted-Reddit recovery, GeoSpy geolocating photos from plants and shadows — next to the defense: a de-dox checklist written after Meta AI inferred a creator's home from old posts, a data-broker opt-out game, the Flock plate-search transparency site. An agent with a weekly cron can run the offense against you and file the defense automatically. The same tools that took a security team now fit in one scheduled skill.
why_it_matters: Anyone posting publicly — creators, small founders, people leaving bad situations — is now one multimodal model away from being located. A self-run sentinel turns a one-time checklist into continuous monitoring, and the opt-out drafting is exactly the tedious work agents are good at.
novelty: The OSINT posts frame themselves as offense or curiosity; the privacy posts frame themselves as a manual checklist. None combine them into a recurring, agent-run loop, and none use the photo-geolocation tools defensively on your own feed.

Schedule it weekly, diff against last run, and have the agent draft data-broker opt-out requests from the checklist for each new hit
Falsifier: if three consecutive weekly runs surface nothing new and the opt-outs stick, a quarterly manual checklist is enough and the agent is overhead
